report.currency: USD (tables in $ millions unless stated; company reports in USD — no FX conversion applied)
report.verdict: A clean, high-quality half: revenue +28.2% reported / +20.8% constant currency to $3,823m, underlying EBITDA +32.8% to $1,921m with a record 50.4% Q2 margin despite a c.2–2.5pp fuel headwind, pre-exceptional EPS +41% to 11.7c and leverage down to 1.6x (0.5x lease-adjusted). The market nonetheless sold the shares c.5.5% to a new 52-week low: capex doubled to $657m, Nigeria decelerated (cc growth 24.4% in Q2 vs 29.8% in Q1, voice revenue down 6% QoQ), $55m of exceptionals hit PAT, and the NGN/ZMW translation tailwind that flattered reported growth expires in Q3. Guidance is unchanged (FY27 capex ~$1.1bn, margins "above 50%", dividend mid-to-high single-digit growth).
summary: **Headline beat on quality, not on narrative.** H1 FY27 (six months to 30 Sep 2026; FYE 31 March) revenue of $3,823m was +28.2% reported and +20.8% constant currency (cc), underlying EBITDA $1,921m (+32.8% / +23.5% cc) at a 50.3% margin (+172bps reported, +109bps cc), PAT $452m (+20.5%), basic EPS 10.2c (+23.3%). No published consensus was available to us; the operating numbers are strong on any reading, but the shares fell c.5.5% on the day (see below).

**Q2 standalone shows the run-rate.** Q2 FY27 revenue $1,970m (+25.7% reported, +20.6% cc, +6.3% QoQ), underlying EBITDA $993m (+29.4% / +22.7% cc, +7.0% QoQ) and a record 50.4% margin (+144bps YoY, +35bps QoQ) despite management saying fuel prices (doubling in Nigeria since April) cost c.2–2.5pp of group margin, c.90% of which was already absorbed in Q2.

**Growth mix: data and mobile money carry the group.** In cc, voice +11.1% ($1,296m), data +28.0% ($1,571m), mobile money +25.8% ($840m segment, $699m post-elimination), other +7.6%. Data is now 50.0% of mobile services revenue (46.5% a year ago). Currency translation added c.$187m to reported revenue (slides) via NGN appreciation (avg 1,360 vs 1,553) and the Zambian kwacha.

**Regional growth is broad but Nigeria decelerated.** H1 cc revenue growth: Nigeria +27.0% ($1,014m, 58.1% EBITDA margin), East Africa +18.2% ($1,777m, 53.6%), Francophone +19.2% ($1,022m, 44.0%). Q2 cc: Nigeria 24.4% (Q1 29.8%) as the Q4 FY25 tariff uplift fully lapped and an airtime-advance partner disruption dragged; East Africa accelerated to 18.6% and Francophone to 20.3%.

**Guidance unchanged — the bridge is flat.** FY27 capex guidance stays at ~$1.1bn (set at FY26 results in May 2026) after H1 capex of $657m (+106.5%), implying H2 of only ~$443m; EBITDA margin commentary is 'above 50%'; dividend policy of mid-to-high single-digit growth reaffirmed with the interim raised 9.2% to 3.1c; the 1% buyback is 67% complete with the remaining 0.33% to resume post close-period. No revenue guidance is given. Management explicitly flagged that the NGN/ZMW lapping benefit ends in Q3, so reported growth will converge toward cc.

**Mobile money is the structural engine and now a listed asset.** Segment revenue $840m (+25.8% cc), customers 60.9m (+22.4%), TPV $130.1bn in H1 (+36.9% cc) and annualised Q2 TPV $275bn (+36.5%); TPV per customer $380/month (+11.7%). Segment EBITDA margin fell 287bps to 48.9% purely because of the renegotiated intra-group agreements (neutral at group level). Mobile money overtook voice in East Africa ($615m vs $593m).

**Airtel Money IPO completed 14 Oct 2026** — 270m existing shares (10%) sold by minority holders at £1.96 (c.£5.3bn / ~$7bn equity value per press reports); Airtel Africa sold nothing and retains 77.85%; 27m-share over-allotment outstanding. The $509m minority put-option liability will be derecognised in H2 with the gain to equity. Airtel Money's own maiden H1 print (per the iBetAfrica piece supplied): revenue $830m (+34% / +25.1% cc), PAT $228m, underlying EBITDA $398m at 48.0% — the $10m gap to the group segment is Nigeria PSB, which sits outside the listed entity.

**Cost efficiency programme (running >2 years) is doing the heavy lifting against fuel.** Levers cited: off-grid-to-grid conversion, solar/battery, AI-driven network energy optimisation, technology modernisation. CFO: at Q4 FY26 fuel prices margins would have been 1.5–2pp higher. Network opex rose to 19.0% of revenue in Q2 from 17.8% in Q1 (our calc) — that is the fuel line; S&M held at 13.2–13.3% of revenue.

**Capex front-loaded; cash conversion lower.** Capex/revenue 17.2% in H1 (10.7% a year ago; 21.0% in Q1, 13.6% in Q2). Operating FCF $1,264m (+12.0%), net cash from operations $1,759m (+26.7%), but management's normalised FCF fell to $280m from $368m after a $713m capex cash payout (incl. $37m Nigeria 900MHz renewal and $65m Kenya 3,500MHz spectrum), $317m cash tax and $430m cash interest.

**Balance sheet keeps improving.** Net debt $5,870m (of which leases $4,497m); leverage 1.6x (2.1x), lease-adjusted net debt $1,373m and 0.5x (0.8x); >95% of OpCo debt in local currency; weighted average cost of debt 10.1% (-231bps). ROCE 25.7% (+543bps). Cash $717m plus $1,489m in mobile money trust (restricted).

**Exceptionals and FX muddy the P&L comparison.** $37m exceptional finance cost (Q1, in-principle settlement of a commercial dispute at a subsidiary) and $19m operating exceptional (Airtel Money IPO costs, Q2), total $55m; FX/derivative gains fell to $2m from $90m. Strip both out and EPS rose to 11.8c from 6.9c (+71%). Underlying finance cost (ex-FX, ex-exceptional) rose to $442m from $394m on $47m higher lease interest from c.2,200 sites added in the period.

**Tax remains the structural drag.** Total tax charge $362m (+29.1%); company-stated effective rate 40.2% (reported tax/PBT 44.5% on our calc) versus a c.32% weighted statutory rate, driven by profit mix and withholding taxes on subsidiary dividends. Contingent liabilities rose $56m to $277m, including a $132m retrospective WHT assessment on historical dividends at one subsidiary (no provision).

**Shareholder returns.** $108.7m returned via buyback (24.5m shares, 0.67% of capital; first tranche completed 28 Sep 2026; average c.$4.44/share); interim DPS 3.1c (+9.2%, record 13 Nov, paid 11 Dec 2026); $155m dividends paid to owners and $45m to NCI in H1. Nigeria is expected to turn retained-earnings positive this calendar year, allowing dividend upstreaming from 2027.

**Strategy/new businesses.** c.4,200 sites added over 12 months, 4,400 additional 4G sites, 99.2% of sites 4G-enabled, 4,094 5G sites across seven markets (5G launched in Gabon and Seychelles), fibre >83,000km. MyAirtel app MAU 14m (8m), app TPV $7.7bn in H1 (+75%). Enterprise base +~60%. Three data centres (Lagos 38MW under construction, Kenya 44MW broken ground, DRC 9MW land acquired). Starlink partnership covers backhaul, enterprise and early direct-to-device in DRC/Uganda under the Airtel brand.

**Governance refresh.** Gopal Vittal became non-executive chair on 9 Jul 2026 (Sunil Bharti Mittal retired as chair), Shravin Bharti Mittal deputy chair, Annika Poutiainen retired, V.K. Viswanathan appointed INED (22 Jul 2026). Regulatory items: Nigeria 900MHz renewed ($37m, 10 years); Kenya 100MHz of 3,500MHz ($65m, 25 years); ongoing engagement on Uganda 90% coverage obligations and Nigeria tariff adjustments (no new increase secured).

**Share price reaction: sell-the-news.** Shares fell c.5.5% to ~259p on 30 Oct 2026 (secondary sources; another cites -5.3%), reversing an early rally to 282p and marking a new 52-week low intraday. The debate is valuation versus capex intensity and Nigeria momentum, not the quality of the H1 numbers.

**Thesis read-through.** The two-engine model (mobile services 5-year revenue CAGR 18.4%; mobile money 28.8%) is intact and operating leverage is visible (EBITDA growing faster than revenue in cc), but H2 reported growth decelerates mechanically as FX lapping ends, Nigeria's price-led growth normalises toward volume-led growth, and the capex step-up compresses FCF. The listed Airtel Money stake (77.85% of a c.£5.3bn IPO valuation ≈ £4.1bn vs AAF market cap of ~£9.4bn at 259p, our estimate) now provides a hard valuation marker for the sum-of-the-parts debate.

segments.name: Mobile services (Nigeria, East Africa, Francophone Africa telecoms)
segments.headline: Data is now half of mobile-services revenue; margin +258bps to 50.5% despite doubled fuel costs, with capex up 115% to $614m.
narrative: Mobile services revenue rose 25.9% in reported currency and 18.9% in constant currency to $3,141m in H1, with Q2 at $1,614m (+23.8% reported, +18.8% cc, +5.6% QoQ). The split is instructive: voice grew 11.1% cc to $1,296m almost entirely on the 11.6% customer base expansion (voice ARPU -0.4% cc at $1.1; total minutes +5.7%; usage flat at 278 minutes per month), while data grew 28.0% cc to $1,571m on a combination of 15.0% more data customers (89.9m) and 10.7% higher data ARPU ($3.0, +17.1% reported). Data crossed the symbolic threshold of 50.0% of segment revenue (46.5% a year ago; 50.9% in Q2 alone). Other revenue of $274m grew 11.4% cc but slowed to 5.6% in Q2.

The volume-versus-price picture is clean. Smartphone penetration rose 4.8pp to 51.6% (over 100m smartphones on network), smartphone data usage reached 13.3GB per month from 10.1GB (12.5GB in Q1), and management's 'more-for-more' pricing means revenue per GB falls as consumption rises — which is why data ARPU growth (10.7%) lags usage growth (c.32%). They framed this as deliberate: recruit at the low end, let consumption migrate up. The group also reports c.71m 4G/5G data customers against a 194m base, so the conversion runway is the core of the equity story.

Underlying EBITDA was $1,586m (+32.7% reported, +24.4% cc) at a 50.5% margin, +258bps reported and +222bps cc; Q2 was 50.8% (+199bps YoY, c.+70bps QoQ). This was delivered while fuel prices roughly doubled in Nigeria and rose across the footprint; at group level the CFO quantified the fuel drag at 2–2.5pp of margin, c.90% of which is already in Q2, and said margins would have been 1.5–2pp higher at Q4 FY26 fuel prices. Sequentially the regional picture diverged: East Africa's mobile services margin jumped 350bps QoQ to 52.2%, while Nigeria fell 130bps to 57.5% (58.8% in Q1) and Francophone fell 120bps to 39.9% as fuel hit. The mitigants are the energy programme (grid conversion, solar/battery, AI network optimisation, equipment modernisation) and operating leverage.

By region (mobile services only), Nigeria revenue was $1,008m (+44.6% reported, +26.6% cc) with Q2 cc growth of 24.0% versus 29.4% in Q1 as the Q4 FY25 tariff adjustments fully lapped; East Africa $1,258m (+20.2% / +15.4% cc) with Q2 accelerating to 16.4%; Francophone $867m (+15.8% / +15.3% cc) with Q2 at 16.5% from 14.0% in Q1. Regional H1 EBITDA margins were 58.2% (+181bps), 50.5% (+225bps) and 40.5% (+93bps) respectively. The Nigeria sequential softness — voice revenue down 6.3% QoQ in USD, data customers up only 0.4m QoQ — is the one blemish, attributed to the airtime-advance partner changes forced by regulation and the pricing lap rather than competition, which management described as rational with no price war.

Capex more than doubled to $614m (+115.1%), equivalent to 19.5% of segment revenue versus 11.4% a year earlier, with Q2 ($246m) well below Q1 ($368m) — the front-loading the CFO described. Roughly 4,200 sites were added over the last twelve months (c.2,200 in the half), plus 4,400 additional 4G sites; 99.2% of sites are 4G-enabled, 5G is live at 4,094 sites across seven markets (3,609 at June) including new launches in Gabon and Seychelles, and fibre exceeds 83,000km. Operating free cash flow still grew 6.8% to $972m (Q2 $575m, +23.8% YoY) because EBITDA growth outran the capex step-up, but the D&A line (+25.4% to $587m) and lease interest (+$47m at group level) are the lagging costs of this build. Adjacent businesses — home broadband (c.3% penetration across the footprint against >30m households with affordability), enterprise (customer base +~60%), Nxtra data centres and Telesonic — remain small but are where incremental capex is being pointed.

segments.name: Mobile money (Airtel Money, all 14 OpCos incl. Nigeria PSB)
segments.headline: Revenue +25.8% cc to $840m on 22.4% customer growth and 37% TPV growth; margin -287bps to 48.9% is the intra-group repricing, not deterioration; now separately listed (AAF retains 77.85%).
narrative: Mobile money revenue was $840m in H1 (+34.8% reported, +25.8% cc) and $437m in Q2 (+31.3% / +25.8% cc, +8.2% QoQ), with the cc growth rate identical across Q1, Q2 and H1 — a remarkably stable 25.8%. Post inter-segment elimination (the cross-charge to mobile services), revenue was $699m against $494m. The customer base grew 22.4% to 60.9m (+7.8% QoQ, i.e. 4.4m net adds in the quarter), lifting mobile money penetration of the telco base by 2.8pp to 31.4%, while cc ARPU rose only 2.6% to $2.5 (+10.0% reported) because the renegotiated intra-group agreements depress both revenue and ARPU. Management keeps pointing to the 133m Airtel telecom customers not yet on the wallet as the acquisition pool.

Volume is the story. Total processed value reached $130.1bn in H1 (+46.4% reported, +36.9% cc) and $68.6bn in Q2 (+42.1% / +36.5% cc, +11.7% QoQ), giving an annualised Q2 run-rate of $275bn versus 'over $245bn' at Q1 and $196bn for FY26. TPV per customer rose 11.7% to $380 per month. By product, wallet services (cash-in/cash-out) grew 27.6% cc to $409m, payments and transfers 29.8% to $363m (33.2% in Q2 — the fastest-growing large line), and financial services 56.9% to $45m, lifting the financial-services share of revenue to 5.4% from 4.3%; the 'others' line (retention revenue from mobile services) fell 40.7% to $23m, again a function of the intra-group changes. The implied take rate (segment revenue/TPV) is c.0.65% and drifting down as payments and transfers outgrow cash-out — the same dynamic the market flagged in Airtel Money's own post-IPO print.

Distribution and digital adoption are the enablers: active agents exceeded 2.5m (+25.3%), exclusive retail touchpoints 48,000, active merchants 587,000 (+85.5%) on interoperable QR, tap-and-pay and payment links, app-transacting customers 6.6m with app penetration of the smartphone base at 19.9% (14.6%), and smartphone users over 54% of the mobile money base. App and multi-service customers carry higher ARPU, which is why the growth algorithm is engagement-led rather than purely acquisition-led. Regionally, East Africa generated $615m (+20.5% cc; 44.1m customers, +13.5%) — now larger than East Africa voice revenue — Francophone $215m (+40.2% cc; 12.6m customers, +41.9%, 10.5% QoQ) driven by DRC, and Nigeria (PSB) $10m from 4.2m customers (+110.9%), still immaterial.

Underlying EBITDA was $411m (+27.4% reported, +17.2% cc) at a 48.9% margin, down 287bps reported and 359bps cc; Q2 was 48.7% (-223bps YoY, c.-40bps QoQ). Management attributes the whole decline to the July 2025 renegotiation of intra-group agreements with mobile services, which is margin-neutral at group level and was pre-disclosed; the lap completes in Q3, after which segment margin comparisons normalise. Capex is trivial ($25m), so operating free cash flow of $386m (+29.0%) converts c.94% of EBITDA. D&A rose 63% to $22m and the segment absorbed $6m of the IPO exceptional costs, leaving operating profit at $374m (+24.0%).

The structural change is the 14 October 2026 London listing of Airtel Mobile Commerce N.V.: 270m existing shares (10%) sold by minority holders at £1.96, implying c.£5.3bn (~$7bn per press reports) of equity value, with Airtel Africa selling nothing and retaining 77.85%; a 27m-share over-allotment is outstanding. The minority put option ($509m liability at 30 September) ceases to be exercisable and will be derecognised in H2 with the gain to equity. Airtel Money's standalone maiden H1 figures (per the user-supplied iBetAfrica article; not verified against the Airtel Money release) were revenue $830m (+34% / +25.1% cc), 56.7m customers, TPV $128bn, PAT $228m and underlying EBITDA $398m at 48.0% (50.8% prior) — the $10m revenue and 4.2m customer gap to the group segment is Nigeria PSB, which sits outside the listed perimeter; the EBITDA definitions do not reconcile exactly and we have not attempted to bridge them. Operating relationships are unchanged and on arm's-length terms; AAF shareholders retain c.78% of the economics and now have a listed valuation reference.

segments.name: Nigeria (mobile services + Airtel Money PSB)
segments.headline: Still the fastest-growing region (+27.0% cc) at a 58.1% margin, but Q2 decelerated to +24.4% cc as the tariff uplift lapped, fuel doubled and the airtime-advance disruption bit; 26.5% of group revenue.
narrative: Nigeria delivered H1 revenue of $1,014m, up 45.0% reported and 27.0% in constant currency, with the gap explained by naira appreciation (weighted average NGN/USD 1,360 versus 1,553 a year earlier; 1,367 in Q1). Q2 revenue of $514m grew 40.2% reported and 24.4% cc but only 2.6% QoQ, and the cc growth rate stepped down from 29.8% in Q1 — the first clear deceleration since the Q4 FY25 tariff adjustments, whose full effect landed in Q2 FY26 and has now fully lapped. Voice revenue of $370m grew 20.6% cc (voice ARPU +7.0%, customers +15.1%) but fell 6.3% QoQ in USD terms to $179m, which management attributed to the regulator-mandated change of airtime-advance partners: new lenders took longer than expected to stabilise and customers temporarily lost access to airtime credit. They say operations are now normalising.

Data remains the engine: revenue of $544m grew 33.8% cc (52.7% reported) on data customers +11.8% to 32.9m and data ARPU +20.5% cc, with smartphone penetration at 56.8% (+4.0pp; the highest in the group) and smartphone usage at 16.7GB per month from 12.7GB. But the Q2 data cc growth rate of 30.1% compares with 38.0% in Q1, data customers rose only 0.4m QoQ against 1.6m total net adds, and mobile services ARPU growth slowed to 8.4% cc in Q2 from 16.5% in Q1. Management's explanation is the 'more-for-more' pricing model — new customers enter at lower consumption and heavy users see revenue per GB fall — plus home broadband and B2B initiatives that are still small. They insist competition is rational with no price war, and that engagement with the NCC on further tariff adjustments continues with no minimum interval constraint, but no new increase is in hand.

Profitability is the group's best. H1 underlying EBITDA was $589m (+50.2% reported, +31.5% cc) at a 58.1% margin (+199bps). Fuel prices doubled since the start of the financial year and the impact built progressively; Q2 absorbed the full effect, with the mobile services margin declining c.130bps sequentially to 57.5% from 58.8% (regional margin including PSB: 57.6% from 58.6%) — the cost efficiency programme limited the damage but did not eliminate it. Capex for mobile services was $177m (+139.9%), heavily Q1-weighted ($128m then $50m), and operating free cash flow rose 28.2% to $409m. Nigeria represents 26.5% of group revenue, which management cites as evidence the portfolio is balanced against single-currency shocks.

Two items matter beyond the P&L. First, the 900MHz licence was renewed for $37m (payable in naira) for ten years. Second, the CFO said Nigeria should turn retained-earnings positive this calendar year after the post-devaluation losses, enabling dividend upstreaming from 2027 if currencies stay stable — a meaningful change in the cash story for a market that has been a trapped-cash problem since 2023. The Nigeria PSB (SmartCash) remains a rounding error at $10m revenue and 4.2m customers but is doubling.

segments.name: East Africa (Kenya, Malawi, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia)
segments.headline: Largest region (46.5% of revenue) accelerated to +18.6% cc in Q2 with a 54.6% margin; mobile money ($615m) now exceeds voice ($593m).
narrative: East Africa revenue rose 24.8% reported and 18.2% in constant currency to $1,777m, with the reported premium driven by Zambian kwacha appreciation. Q2 revenue of $923m grew 22.3% reported, 18.6% cc and 8.1% QoQ — the fastest sequential growth of the three regions and an acceleration from 17.8% cc in Q1 despite what management called a high base. The composition is the most balanced in the group: voice $593m (+8.9% cc, essentially the 8.0% customer growth), data $566m (+26.0% cc; 29.4% in Q2), mobile money $615m (+20.5% cc) and other $89m (-2.7% cc, -11.0% in Q2). The milestone is that mobile money revenue overtook voice in the half.

Within mobile services, revenue of $1,258m grew 15.4% cc (16.4% in Q2) on customers +8.0% to 88.8m and ARPU +6.1% cc to $2.4. Data customers rose 15.2% to 39.5m, data ARPU +8.1% cc, smartphone penetration +4.9pp to 48.6% (the lowest of the three regions, hence the longest runway) and smartphone usage 12.2GB per month from 9.0GB. Mobile money customers grew 13.5% to 44.1m — slower than the group's 22.4% because this is the most penetrated region — so growth here is engagement-led (payments and transfers, financial services).

Regional underlying EBITDA was $953m (+26.0% reported, +18.2% cc) at a 53.6% margin, +54bps reported but -1bp cc, which tells you the reported margin expansion is partly a kwacha effect. The mobile services margin, however, rose 225bps to 50.5% (211bps cc) and jumped 350bps QoQ to 52.2% in Q2 — East Africa appears to have handled the fuel shock far better than Nigeria or Francophone, helped by grid access and the efficiency programme. Q2 regional margin was 54.6% (+57bps YoY, +210bps QoQ).

Mobile services capex nearly doubled to $247m (+98.9%; $138m in Q1, $109m in Q2) and included the Kenya acquisition of 100MHz of 3,500MHz spectrum for $65m over 25 years (a 5G/fixed-wireless enabler). Operating free cash flow was nonetheless broadly stable at $388m (+2.0%), and Q2 OpFCF of $231m was +19.1% YoY. The Nxtra 44MW Kenya data centre (the largest in East Africa, per management) has broken ground. The open regulatory item is Uganda's 90% coverage obligation; management says engagement continues, rollout plans demonstrate commitment and no material repercussions are anticipated — we would still treat it as a capex/timing risk rather than a solved issue.

segments.name: Francophone Africa (Chad, DRC, Gabon, Madagascar, Niger, Rep. of Congo, Seychelles)
segments.headline: Turnaround sustained: cc growth accelerated to +20.3% in Q2 with mobile money +40%; margin flat at 44.0% as fuel offset operating leverage; OpFCF -21.6% on doubled capex.
narrative: Francophone revenue was $1,022m, up 19.6% reported and 19.2% cc — the one region where reported and constant-currency growth are aligned (CFA/euro peg). Q2 revenue of $529m grew 19.5% reported, 20.3% cc and 7.5% QoQ, up from 18.0% cc in Q1, which management flagged as a milestone for a region that was the group's laggard three years ago. Mobile money is the standout at $215m (+40.2% cc; 41.3% in Q2) on customers +41.9% to 12.6m (+10.5% QoQ), led by DRC; data grew 24.0% cc to $461m (26.6% in Q2); voice only 5.5% cc to $334m because interconnect rate cuts pushed voice ARPU down even as customers grew 14.3%; other revenue +5.5% to $64m.

Mobile services revenue was $867m (+15.3% cc; Q2 16.5% from 14.0% in Q1) with the growth entirely volume-driven: customers +14.3% to 43.4m, data customers +21.3% to 17.4m, but mobile services ARPU flat at $3.4 (-0.1% cc). Smartphone penetration rose 5.4pp to 50.2%, smartphone usage reached 9.7GB per month from 7.6GB (the lowest of the regions, so most upside), and 97.4% of sites are now 4G (93.3% a year ago; 94.2% at June) after a heavy 4G overlay. 5G launched in Gabon and the Seychelles in the period.

Regional underlying EBITDA was $450m (+19.5% reported, +19.3% cc) at a 44.0% margin, flat YoY (-4bps reported, +2bps cc) and down 130bps QoQ to 43.4% in Q2 — fuel inflation absorbed the operating leverage. The mobile services margin improved 93bps YoY to 40.5% but fell to 39.9% in Q2 from 41.1% in Q1, again fuel-driven and partly offset by efficiency savings. This remains the lowest-margin region by a wide distance (Nigeria 58%, East Africa 54%), reflecting scale, grid reliability and market structure; the medium-term margin opportunity is here if the revenue momentum holds.

The cost of the turnaround is visible in cash: mobile services capex rose 114.8% to $187m ($102m in Q1, $85m in Q2) and operating free cash flow fell 21.6% to $164m (Q2 $94m, -3.2% YoY). Management's framing is that network investment is what unlocked customer growth across both telecoms and mobile money, and the Q2 acceleration supports that. The DRC 9MW data centre (land acquired) and the Starlink direct-to-device pilot in DRC are the adjacent bets. With 26.7% of group revenue, Francophone is now the same size as Nigeria in revenue terms but earns $139m less EBITDA.

highlights.text: Record Q2 underlying EBITDA margin of 50.4% (+144bps YoY, +35bps QoQ) and H1 50.3% (+172bps) delivered while absorbing a 2–2.5pp fuel headwind — the cost efficiency programme (energy, AI network optimisation, grid/solar conversion) is demonstrably real and the H1 margin would have been 1.5–2pp higher at Q4 FY26 fuel prices.

Mobile money compounding at a steady 25.8% cc with TPV +36.9% cc to $130bn (annualised $275bn), customers +22.4% to 60.9m, merchants +85.5% and financial services revenue +56.9%; now a separately listed asset at c.£5.3bn equity value with AAF retaining 77.85% — a hard SOTP marker.

Data revenue +28.0% cc to $1,571m on 15% more data customers and 10.7% ARPU growth, now 50% of mobile services revenue; smartphone penetration 51.6% with c.71m 4G/5G users on a 194m base leaves a long conversion runway.

Leverage down to 1.6x (0.5x lease-adjusted; lease-adjusted net debt $1,373m from $1,633m), cost of debt -231bps to 10.1%, >95% of OpCo debt in local currency, ROCE 25.7% (+543bps) — the balance sheet can fund the capex step-up and returns simultaneously.

Francophone and East Africa both accelerated in Q2 (cc +20.3% and +18.6%) — group growth is no longer a Nigeria price-increase story; the three regions are each growing 18–27% cc with East Africa's mobile services margin +350bps QoQ.

Nigeria upstreaming: management expects retained earnings to turn positive this calendar year with dividends from Nigeria from 2027, and the 900MHz licence is renewed for ten years at $37m payable in naira — removes a long-standing trapped-cash overhang.

Underlying EPS (pre-exceptional, ex FX/derivative gains) rose 71% to 11.8c from 6.9c; interim DPS +9.2% to 3.1c; $108.7m buyback executed with the final 0.33% tranche to resume and the board to review a further programme on completion.

lowlights.text: Nigeria momentum faded in Q2: cc revenue growth 24.4% vs 29.8% in Q1, data cc growth 30.1% vs 38.0%, mobile services ARPU growth 8.4% vs 16.5%, voice revenue -6.3% QoQ and data net adds of just 0.4m. Management blames the tariff lap, 'more-for-more' pricing and the airtime-advance partner disruption — plausible, but Nigeria has no new tariff approval and fuel there has doubled.

Capex more than doubled to $657m (17.2% of revenue vs 10.7%) and normalised FCF fell to $280m from $368m; D&A +26% and lease interest +$47m are the lagging P&L costs. The ~$1.1bn FY27 guide implies H2 of only ~$443m, which looks optimistic against 'we remain open to possibilities' — upside risk to capex, downside to FCF.

Reported growth has been flattered by NGN (avg 1,360 vs 1,553) and ZMW appreciation (c.$187m of H1 revenue, c.+7.4pp of reported growth); the CFO explicitly said the lapping benefit ends in Q3, so reported revenue/EBITDA growth should step down toward the c.20% cc rate just as the stock derates.

$55m of exceptionals ($37m in-principle settlement of a commercial dispute at an unnamed subsidiary; $19m Airtel Money IPO costs) plus FX/derivative gains collapsing to $2m from $90m; contingent liabilities up $56m to $277m including a $132m retrospective WHT assessment on historical dividends with no provision taken.

Effective tax remains punitive — total tax $362m, company-stated ETR 40.2% (44.5% reported tax/PBT) against a c.32% statutory blend because of profit mix and withholding tax on subsidiary dividends; NCI absorbs 18% of PAT, and the Airtel Money listing institutionalises a c.22% minority leak on the fastest-growing cash stream.

Mobile money segment margin -287bps to 48.9% (Q2 48.7%) from the intra-group repricing, and the implied take rate is drifting down (c.0.65% vs 0.70%) as payments outgrow cash-out — neutral at group level but it is the variable the market will now price in the listed subsidiary.

Francophone remains structurally low-margin (44.0% region, 39.9% mobile services in Q2, -120bps QoQ) and its OpFCF fell 21.6% on doubled capex; Uganda's 90% coverage obligation and Nigeria tariff engagement are unresolved regulatory items.

forecast.intro: There is no formal revenue or EBITDA guidance and nothing changed at this print. The only quantitative guide — FY27 capex of approximately $1.1bn, set at the FY26 results on 8 May 2026 — was reiterated despite H1 spend of $657m (60% of the full-year number), so the arithmetic implies a much lighter H2 of ~$443m; the CEO's 'we remain open to possibilities' leaves the door ajar for an upward revision. On margins, management reiterated 'above 50%' with fuel 90% absorbed in Q2 and only marginal incremental drag expected in Q3 if prices stabilise (though they noted fuel rose again in some markets in the three weeks before the call). The dividend framework (mid-to-high single-digit growth) and the 1% buyback (67% done, 0.33% to resume) are unchanged. The division driving the narrative is mobile services in Nigeria — the deceleration there, rather than any guidance change, is what the market reacted to — while the mobile money segment's intra-group margin lap completes in Q3 and the FX translation tailwind (NGN/ZMW) expires in Q3.

forecast.view: **Our FY27 (Mar-27) estimates (not company guidance): revenue ~$7.9–8.0bn (+24% reported, ~+20% cc), underlying EBITDA ~$4.0bn at a ~50.0–50.5% margin, pre-exceptional EPS ~24–25c (FY26: 18.6c), capex ~$1.1–1.2bn, year-end leverage ~1.5x / ~0.4–0.5x lease-adjusted.** Arithmetic: Q2 revenue $1,970m; with FX lapping gone we assume Q3 ~$2.04bn (+21% YoY on $1,685m) and Q4 ~$2.10bn (+20% on $1,748m), giving H2 ~$4.1bn and FY ~$7.96bn. H2 EBITDA at ~50.2% ≈ $2.08bn (FY ~$4.0bn, +27%); H2 D&A ~$660m, net finance cost ~$450m ex-FX, ETR ~41%, NCI ~18% → H2 attributable ~$470m ≈ 13c on 3.63bn shares, so FY pre-exceptional EPS ≈ 11.7c + 13c ≈ 24–25c and reported EPS ≈ 23c after the $55m H1 exceptionals. **Next quarter (Q3 FY27, Dec-26):** expect cc revenue growth of ~19–20% but reported growth stepping down to ~20–22% from 25.7% as the naira/kwacha comparison normalises; Nigeria cc growth likely settles in the low-20s absent a tariff approval; mobile money segment margin stabilises ~48–49% as the intra-group lap completes; group margin ~50% ±50bps depending on fuel. **Swing factors:** (1) fuel — each 1pp of margin is ~$40m of H2 EBITDA; (2) NGN — a 1% USD move is $66–68m revenue, $33–35m EBITDA and $27–29m finance cost on the company's 12-month sensitivity, with $13–15m of the finance-cost line NGN-specific; (3) Nigeria tariff re-engagement (upside) versus airtime-advance normalisation (recovery); (4) capex creep above $1.1bn; (5) derecognition of the $509m Airtel Money put liability (equity, non-P&L) and the over-allotment outcome; (6) the $132m WHT assessment. **Leverage direction is down** on EBITDA growth even with ~$0.5bn of annual lease additions; the main constraint on cash returns is capex intensity, not the balance sheet. We would want to see Nigeria data net adds and ARPU re-accelerate in Q3 before concluding the Q2 wobble was purely timing.
watch: Nigeria Q3 FY27 cc growth, data net adds and ARPU: does the airtime-advance recovery and 'more-for-more' pricing restore >25% cc growth, and is there any NCC tariff approval?
Fuel/energy cost line (network opex as % of revenue, 19.0% in Q2 vs 17.8% in Q1) and whether the Q3 margin holds ≥50% given renewed fuel increases flagged on the call.
Reported-vs-cc convergence in Q3 as NGN/ZMW lapping ends; any renewed naira or kwacha weakness (company sensitivity: 1% USD move = $33–35m EBITDA).
FY27 capex outturn vs the ~$1.1bn guide (H2 implied ~$443m) and normalised FCF; D&A and lease-interest creep.
Airtel Money post-IPO: over-allotment exercise, derecognition of the $509m put liability, take-rate trajectory and any change to intra-group terms; AAF's 77.85% stake value vs its own market cap.
Resumption and completion of the remaining 0.33% buyback and the board's decision on a further programme; Nigeria dividend upstreaming from 2027.
Contingent liabilities ($277m incl. $132m WHT assessment), Uganda coverage obligations, and identity/terms of the $37m dispute settlement.

The move was attributed to the doubling of capex, Nigeria's sequential deceleration, the $55m exceptional charge and a risk-off tape, rather than to the H1 numbers themselves.
